headline: Plum Gut Goes Quiet — And That's Exactly When the Bass Show Up
subhead: A softening current ahead of Tuesday's neap is turning ripping water into a controllable eel bite, and the fluke never left.
body_markdown:
Three-fifteen a.m., chest waders, standing on the rocks at the Gut with the current still hauling at four knots and a 12-inch eel swimbait on a three-way rig swinging through the seam like it owed me money. Second drift through the heaviest push, right on the tide change, something leaned into it that wasn't playing around — thirty-six inches, thick through the shoulders, came up out of the froth right where the eddy folds back against the rock pile on the west side. That's the fish that tells you the pattern's real, not just a rumor from the bait shop.

Here's the deal on Plum Gut and The Race right now: the water's still ripping hard enough to make boat control a full-time job, but Tuesday's first-quarter neap is already starting to take the edge off. I felt it Thursday night — the same stage of tide that was unmanageable two weeks ago is now giving me a longer window to actually work a presentation instead of just surviving the drift. That's the single biggest thing to know this week. As the current eases through the neap, eel and swimbait presentations get easier to control, and the strike zone stops being a two-minute burst at max flow and starts stretching into a real bite window on either side of the tide change. If you've been getting your teeth kicked in trying to fish the peak of the flood or ebb through the Gut, back off the max-current window and fish the building and softening stages instead — that's where the bass are actually eating right now, not just holding.

The technique that's putting fish on the deck is straightforward and unforgiving: 12-inch eel-style swimbaits or shad-style paddletails on a three-way rig, dropper heavy enough to hold bottom in the current, worked through the deepest, fastest part of the rip right on the tide change. You're not swimming this thing — you're letting the current do the work and controlling depth with your dropper weight. Bass are stacking on the down-current side of the rock piles and current seams where the Gut necks down, and they're eating on the pause, not the retrieve. If you're throwing bucktails instead, 1.5 to 2 ounces, same idea — cast across the seam, let it sink clean off the edge, slow rhythmic lift-and-drop along bottom. That's the pattern that's been working the hard-current edges up and down the East End this month, and Plum Gut is prime water for it because the structure creates so many defined seams to work.

Fluke haven't missed a beat. This has been the most dependable bite in the entire zone — Plum Gut, the flats off Orient, and the channel edges around Fishers Island are all holding keepers mixed into the shorts, and unlike the bass, the fluke never got fussy about the warm surface water. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift over 25 to 40 feet of water on moving tide, keep producing. I had a 28-inch sea bass — a genuine surprise, north of five pounds — come off a rock pile adjacent to the rip on the same drift as a pair of keeper fluke, which tells you the structure right at the mouth of the Gut is holding a real mixed bag right now. Worth working those humps slow and thorough instead of running through them.

Bluefish are the other story worth your time. Jumbo blues are showing on the hard current edges at both the Race and the Gut, slashing through bait right on the surface in visible boils — daylight fish, which isn't always the case with blues this time of year. When you see the boil, don't long-bomb it. Feather a short, accurate cast directly into the seam where the bait's getting pushed, because these fish are locked onto a tight ambush point, not roaming open water. Poppers and metal both work; the key is precision over distance.

Water's telling a clear story on temperature this week — New London's sitting around 70, Montauk's a touch warmer at 71.6, and that gradient is exactly why the Eastern Sound striper bite is holding up better through daylight hours than what guys are dealing with further west and south, where the warmer shallow water has pushed bass into strict low-light and after-dark patterns. Out here, the current and depth at the Gut and the Race are keeping things cool enough that fish will still eat in daylight if you find the right seam — but I'm not going to pretend it's a guarantee. I've had drifts through the peak of the tide this week that produced nothing but current burn on my line, and drifts twenty minutes later on the softening stage that put three fish on deck. Timing inside the tide matters as much as the spot right now.

Looking ahead, I expect that neap tide to keep opening up the window through the middle of the week — Tuesday and Wednesday should give the most forgiving current for anyone running eels or bucktails through the Gut for the first time this season. After that, tides build back toward the full moon and the rip gets mean again, so if you're going to learn this eel-on-a-three-way pattern, this is the stretch to do it. Fluke should stay steady regardless of tide stage; that bite's been resilient all month. Bluefish will keep showing on the surface as long as the bait stays put in the current seams, but that can shut off fast if a blow scatters everything, so don't wait around if you see a boil working — get on it.
